about: Reference shells centred on the Sun, drawn as three great circles each (ecliptic plane and two perpendicular planes) with one label.

shells.label: Heliopause · 120 AU
shells.source: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause at 121.6 AU in August 2012 and Voyager 2 at 119 AU in November 2018 (NASA/JPL). The real boundary is not a sphere.
shells.description: Where the solar wind stops against the gas between the stars. Interstellar space begins here, but the Sun's gravity rules for a thousand times farther.

shells.label: Solar gravity lens focus · 550 AU
shells.source: Eshleman (1979, Science 205, 1133): light grazing the Sun's edge comes to a focus from about 548 AU outward.
shells.description: From here outward the Sun's gravity focuses the light of whatever lies exactly behind it: a telescope placed here could map the surface of an exoplanet.

shells.label: 1,000 AU · 5.8 light-days
shells.description: About where the inner edge of the Oort Cloud is usually put (1,000-2,000 AU). Voyager 1 will get here in about 300 years.

shells.label: 10,000 AU · 58 light-days
shells.description: The heart of the inner Oort Cloud. An orbit this size takes a million years.

shells.label: 1 light-year · 63,241 AU
shells.description: One light-year from the Sun: still inside the outer Oort Cloud.

shells.label: 100,000 AU · 1.58 light-years
shells.source: Exact distance; as an edge it is nominal. The Sun's tidal (Jacobi) radius in the Galaxy is about 1.4 pc (280,000 AU) towards the Galactic centre, for Oort constants A = 15.3 and B = -11.9 km/s/kpc (Bovy 2017).
shells.description: The nominal outer edge of the Oort Cloud. Comets this far out are held so weakly that the Galaxy's tide and passing stars strip them away. Voyager 1 needs about 30,000 years to get past here.

voyager.source: NASA/JPL (Voyager mission status and 'Oort Cloud' fact sheet): about 300 years to reach the inner edge of the Oort Cloud and about 30,000 years to fly beyond it
